11-system-design/case-07-ride-hailing-pl.title: Case Study 7: Ride-Hailing Full Data Platform (Uber-style) — Architect-Level Scope
11-system-design/case-07-ride-hailing-pl.tagline: *This case study operates at a broader ARCHITECT-level scope (recap file 9) than the others — designing the OVERALL data platform strategy a…
learnItems: Overview
Step 1: Requirements (Organizational Scope)
Step 2: The Organizational + Technical Architecture
Step 3: Capacity Estimation (Organizational Scale)
Step 4: Technology/Governance Choices, Justified

steps.heading: Overview
steps.body: *This case study operates at a broader ARCHITECT-level scope (recap file 9) than the others — designing the OVERALL data platform strategy across multiple teams/systems, not just one pipeline.*

steps.heading: Step 1: Requirements (Organizational Scope)
steps.body:
```
Business context: a ride-hailing company has grown from a startup (one
  small data team, one Postgres database) to a mid-size company with
  MULTIPLE product teams (rider app, driver app, pricing/surge team,
  safety team, finance) each wanting their own data needs served,
  currently creating duplicated, inconsistent pipelines and growing
  data warehouse costs with no clear ownership model.

Architect-level requirements:
  - Enable MULTIPLE teams to build their own data pipelines/models
    WITHOUT creating a bottleneck on one central data team (recap
    file 3's Data Mesh discussion)
  - Establish CONSISTENT definitions for core business metrics (recap
    `09-visualization/06`'s semantic layer discussion) so "active
    driver" means the SAME thing across pricing, safety, and finance teams
  - Real-time needs (matching, surge pricing) MUST coexist with batch
    analytics needs (financial reporting, growth metrics) — recap
    the ride-hailing DATABASE case study (`05-databases/case-studies/`),
    now extended to the FULL data platform level
  - Cost governance — as pipeline count grows across teams, cost
    accountability (recap `07-cloud-platforms/08`'s FinOps) must scale too
```

steps.heading: Step 2: The Organizational + Technical Architecture
steps.body:
```
                    ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
                    │   PLATFORM TEAM (shared foundation)    │
                    │  - Kafka infrastructure (event backbone)│
                    │  - Warehouse infrastructure (Snowflake) │
                    │  - dbt Semantic Layer (core metric      │
                    │    definitions: "active driver",        │
                    │    "completed trip", "surge multiplier")│
                    │  - Orchestration platform (Airflow,      │
                    │    shared, metadata-driven per           │
                    │    `08-orchestration/case-studies/`)      │
                    │  - Data catalog/governance standards      │
                    └─────────────────────────────────────┘
                                      |
        ┌─────────────────┬──────────┴──────────┬─────────────────┐
        v                 v                     v                 v
  Pricing Team      Safety Team           Finance Team      Growth Team
  (owns their OWN   (owns their OWN       (owns their OWN   (owns their OWN
   dbt models for    dbt models for        dbt models for    dbt models for
   surge/matching    incident detection    revenue/payout     activation/
   data, using        models, using         reconciliation,    retention
   shared real-time   shared event data)    using shared       metrics, using
   event backbone)                          warehouse infra)   shared infra)
```
**Key architectural insight (this is the CORE of what makes this an architect-level, not senior-engineer-level, problem)**: the design decision isn't "which database/streaming tool" — it's ORGANIZATIONAL: a Data Mesh-inspired model where a PLATFORM team provides shared, well-governed INFRASTRUCTURE and CORE metric definitions, while INDIVIDUAL product teams own their OWN domain-specific pipelines/models on top of that shared foundation — directly solving the stated "one central team is a bottleneck" problem while maintaining consistency where it matters most (core metrics).

steps.heading: Step 3: Capacity Estimation (Organizational Scale)
steps.body:
```
At this company's scale (recap the ride-hailing DATABASE case study's
  numbers): millions of location pings/minute, hundreds of thousands of
  trips/day across the core event backbone — but the ARCHITECT-level
  estimation question is different: "how many PIPELINES/dbt models
  will exist across ALL teams in 2 years, and does our platform
  (Airflow scheduler capacity, dbt project structure, warehouse compute)
  scale to support DOZENS of teams each building 10-50 models, not just
  ONE team's needs?" — this is capacity planning for ORGANIZATIONAL
  GROWTH, not just data volume growth.
```

steps.heading: Step 4: Technology/Governance Choices, Justified
steps.body:
**A dbt Semantic Layer for CORE cross-team metrics, but NOT for every team-specific metric**

**Shared Kafka event backbone, team-owned downstream consumers**
> Justification: recap file 3's event-driven architecture pattern — the core trip/location event stream is produced ONCE by the platform team, and EACH product team (pricing, safety) builds their OWN consumer logic independently, without needing the platform team to build custom integration for each team's specific need.

**A metadata-driven, shared Airflow platform (recap `08-orchestration/case-studies/`) rather than each team running its own separate orchestrator**
> Justification: avoids the operational overhead/cost of MULTIPLE teams each maintaining their own Airflow deployment, while the metadata-driven pattern lets each team register their OWN DAGs/pipelines without needing platform-team approval for every single new pipeline — balancing shared infrastructure efficiency against team autonomy.

**A lightweight architectural review process for NEW shared infrastructure decisions (not for every individual pipeline)**
> Justification: the architect-level judgment here is deciding WHAT requires cross-team review (e.g., "should we adopt a new warehouse technology," "should we change the core event schema") vs what teams should decide autonomously (their own specific dbt models/dashboards) — over-governing everything recreates the bottleneck; under-governing shared/foundational decisions risks fragmentation.

callout.label: GOOD TO KNOW
callout.text: Justification: recap `09-visualization/06` — the semantic layer solves metric INCONSISTENCY specifically for metrics MULTIPLE teams need to agree on (revenue, active drivers); forcing EVERY team-specific metric through central semantic layer governance would recreate the exact central-bottleneck problem this architecture is meant to solve. The judgment call here — WHICH metrics need central governance vs which can be team-owned — is itself a genuinely architect-level decision.

steps.heading: Step 5: Failure Modes & Scale (Organizational)
steps.body:
```
"What happens when Team A's dbt model changes a shared upstream table's
schema, breaking Team B's downstream model?"
  -> Directly connects to file 5's data contract discussion — this
     needs an explicit, ENFORCED schema change/review process for
     shared tables specifically (not every table), with the semantic
     layer's core metrics given the STRICTEST protection since the
     most teams depend on them.

"How do you prevent cost from spiraling as team count and pipeline
count both grow?"
  -> Recap `07-cloud-platforms/08`'s FinOps tagging discipline, applied
     ORGANIZATIONALLY: every team's warehouse usage/pipelines are
     tagged by team, with visible cost dashboards PER team (chargeback/
     showback) — making cost a visible, owned concern for each team,
     not an opaque central platform-team problem alone.

"A new team (e.g., a new 'insurance products' team) joins — how do
they onboard onto this platform?"
  -> A genuinely architect-level concern: is there DOCUMENTED,
     SELF-SERVICE onboarding (a template dbt project structure, clear
     platform documentation, a "how to register a new DAG" guide) or
     does every new team require bespoke, time-consuming platform-team
     hand-holding? — the ANSWER to this question is itself a measure
     of whether this architecture will genuinely scale organizationally,
     not just technically.
```

callout.label: GOOD TO KNOW
callout.text: "Given the organizational bottleneck problem (one central team, multiple product teams needing data capability), I'm proposing a Data Mesh-inspired architecture: a platform team providing shared infrastructure (Kafka, warehouse, orchestration) and a semantic layer for CORE cross-team metrics specifically, while individual product teams own their own domain-specific pipelines on top of that foundation. The central tradeoff is accepting LESS centralized control over team-specific data logic in exchange for removing the central-team bottleneck — justified because the stated problem is explicitly about team velocity being blocked by centralization. This only works with genuine organizational discipline: clear standards for what requires cross-team review (core metrics, shared schemas) versus team autonomy (their own models/dashboards), and self-service onboarding documentation so this scales to new teams without constant platform-team hand-holding."

steps.heading: Why This Case Study Is Different From the Other 6
steps.body:
```
Case studies 1-6 each design ONE coherent system/pipeline for a specific
technical requirement. This case study operates at the SCOPE described
in file 9's "Data Architect" description — designing not just a
pipeline, but the ORGANIZATIONAL STRUCTURE and GOVERNANCE MODEL under
which MANY teams' pipelines coexist — precisely the kind of problem
that separates Senior Data Engineer interviews from Staff/Principal/
Architect-level interviews, and exactly why this module exists.
```

12-interview-prep/01-interview-process-o.title: The Interview Process — What to Actually Expect
12-interview-prep/01-interview-process-o.tagline: 1. RESUME SCREEN (recruiter or ATS) — 30 seconds to 2 minutes of actual
learnItems: The Typical Data Engineering Interview Pipeline (product/tech companies)
What Each Stage Is ACTUALLY Testing (beyond the surface topic)
How Long This Actually Takes (set realistic expectations)
Remote/Virtual Interview-Specific Practical Tips
Interview Traps

steps.heading: The Typical Data Engineering Interview Pipeline (product/tech companies)
steps.body:
```
1. RESUME SCREEN (recruiter or ATS) — 30 seconds to 2 minutes of actual
   human attention, if it gets past automated keyword filtering at all

2. RECRUITER SCREEN (15-30 min, phone/video) — basic fit check: are
   your skills/experience roughly aligned, salary expectations, notice
   period, work authorization

3. TECHNICAL SCREEN (45-60 min, often with a senior IC, not the
   hiring manager) — usually SQL + Python live coding, sometimes a
   quick system design warm-up question

4. ONSITE / VIRTUAL ONSITE LOOP (3-5 rounds, often same day or spread
   across a week):
   - SQL/coding round (deeper than the screen)
   - System design round (see module 11, applied live)
   - Behavioral round (see file 3)
   - "Bar raiser" / culture-fit round (varies by company)
   - Sometimes a take-home assignment REPLACES one or more of the
     above, reviewed in a follow-up discussion round

5. HIRING MANAGER / TEAM FIT (often a less formal conversation, but
   genuinely evaluative — "would I want to work with this person")

6. REFERENCE CHECKS + OFFER
```
**Real variation**: startups often COMPRESS this (fewer, more informal rounds); large enterprises often EXTEND it (more rounds, more formal rubrics, sometimes a separate "values" interview) — always ask the recruiter directly what THEIR specific process looks like rather than assuming.

steps.heading: What Each Stage Is ACTUALLY Testing (beyond the surface topic)
steps.body:
```
Recruiter screen: mostly LOGISTICS fit, but also basic COMMUNICATION —
  can you explain your background clearly and concisely? A rambling,
  unfocused answer here can genuinely end the process early, regardless
  of technical skill.

Technical screen (SQL/Python): NOT just "do you know the syntax" — also
  testing whether you can work through a problem OUT LOUD, handle being
  slightly stuck without freezing, and communicate your reasoning as you go.

System design round: testing JUDGMENT (module 11) far more than
  encyclopedic tool knowledge — the interviewer usually cares MORE about
  your requirements-gathering and tradeoff reasoning than whether you
  picked the exact tool they had in mind.

Behavioral round: testing whether you'll be a GOOD TEAMMATE and whether
  your past behavior predicts good future behavior in THIS specific
  role/team — genuine self-awareness and honest reflection score far
  better than a rehearsed "perfect" story with no real learning shown.

"Bar raiser" / senior-level rounds: often SPECIFICALLY testing whether
  you'd raise the technical/cultural bar of the team, not just meet the
  minimum — expect deeper "why" follow-up questions probing your
  actual understanding, not just your ability to recite a concept.
```

steps.heading: How Long This Actually Takes (set realistic expectations)
steps.body:
```
From first application to signed offer: commonly 3-8 WEEKS at a
  reasonably responsive company, sometimes considerably longer at
  large enterprises with more approval layers — genuinely useful to
  know so you don't panic or assume rejection from normal process delay.
```

steps.heading: Remote/Virtual Interview-Specific Practical Tips
steps.body:
```
- Test your screen-share/whiteboard tool BEFORE the interview starts,
  not during it
- Have a notepad/scratch document ready for system design sketching if
  no shared whiteboard tool is provided
- Genuinely OK to ask "can you repeat/clarify the question" — much
  better than answering the wrong question confidently
```

steps.heading: Interview Traps
steps.body:
- Don't treat the recruiter screen as unimportant "just logistics" — genuine communication clarity here sets the tone for how the rest of your candidacy is perceived internally before you even reach a technical round.
- If you don't know what a specific company's process looks like, ASK the recruiter directly — this is a completely normal, expected question, not a sign of weakness.

12-interview-prep/02-resume-and-portfoli.title: Resume & Portfolio — Getting Past the Screen
12-interview-prep/02-resume-and-portfoli.tagline: A recruiter/ATS spends SECONDS, not minutes, on an initial resume scan.
learnItems: The Brutal Reality of Resume Screening
Structuring a Data Engineering Resume
Writing Impact-Focused Bullet Points (the single highest-leverage resume skill)
The GitHub Portfolio — Genuinely Important for Data Engineers Specifically
Tailoring Your Resume Per Application (worth the extra effort)

steps.heading: The Brutal Reality of Resume Screening
steps.body:
```
A recruiter/ATS spends SECONDS, not minutes, on an initial resume scan.
Your resume's job is NOT to prove you're qualified in exhaustive detail —
it's to get you to the NEXT stage where a human actually talks to you.
Every design/content decision should serve THAT specific goal.
```

steps.heading: Structuring a Data Engineering Resume
steps.body:
```
1. Header: name, contact, LinkedIn, GitHub (a real, populated GitHub
   matters more for DE roles than most other fields — see Portfolio below)

2. Summary (optional, 2-3 lines MAX if included): only worth including
   if it adds genuine specific value ("Data Engineer with 4 years
   building cloud-native pipelines processing 10TB+/day on AWS"),
   never generic filler ("hardworking team player passionate about data")

3. Technical Skills: organized by CATEGORY (Languages, Cloud, Big Data,
   Orchestration, Databases) — not just a flat wall of buzzwords;
   matching the categories a job posting/ATS is likely scanning for

4. Experience: REVERSE chronological, each bullet point ideally
   following an IMPACT-focused structure (see below), not a duty-listing structure

5. Projects (especially valuable if experience is limited): real,
   working projects with clear descriptions and GitHub links

6. Education/Certifications: relevant certs (cloud platform certs
   genuinely help for DE roles specifically, more than many other fields)
```

steps.heading: Writing Impact-Focused Bullet Points (the single highest-leverage resume skill)
steps.body:
```
WEAK (duty-listing, no impact shown):
  "Responsible for building ETL pipelines using Airflow and Spark"

STRONG (impact-focused, quantified where possible):
  "Redesigned a nightly ETL pipeline using Airflow + Spark, reducing
  runtime from 6 hours to 45 minutes and cutting AWS compute costs by 40%"

The STRUCTURE: [Action verb] + [what you built/did] + [quantified
  impact/result] — even if you can't get an exact number, a directional
  claim ("significantly reduced," "enabled the team to X") is far
  stronger than a pure duty description with no outcome mentioned at all.
```

steps.heading: The GitHub Portfolio — Genuinely Important for Data Engineers Specifically
steps.body:
```
Unlike many roles, Data Engineering hiring managers OFTEN actually look
at a candidate's GitHub — it's concrete, verifiable evidence of real skill.

What a GOOD DE portfolio project looks like:
- A REAL end-to-end pipeline (not just a single Jupyter notebook) —
  ideally touching several skills from this repo: extraction, a proper
  data model, transformation (dbt/Spark), orchestration (Airflow), and
  IDEALLY some cloud component
- A clear, well-written README explaining WHAT it does, WHY you built
  it that way (a mini version of module 11's tradeoff reasoning!), and
  HOW to run it
- Clean, readable code — remember, someone MIGHT actually open these
  files during your interview process
- Evidence of testing/CI (even a simple GitHub Actions workflow, recap
  `10-devops/06`) signals real production-mindset maturity beyond just
  "I can write a script"

What to AVOID:
- A GitHub full of abandoned, half-finished tutorial-following repos
  with no original thought/README
- Copy-pasted boilerplate with no genuine understanding demonstrated
- Committed credentials/secrets (a genuine, embarrassing real mistake —
  recap `10-devops/02`'s .gitignore discussion)
```

steps.heading: Tailoring Your Resume Per Application (worth the extra effort)
steps.body:
```
A GENERIC resume sent to every job posting performs worse than a
resume LIGHTLY tailored to emphasize the specific skills/tools each
job posting mentions — this doesn't mean fabricating experience, it
means genuinely EMPHASIZING the most relevant parts of your real
experience for THIS specific role (e.g., leading with your Azure
experience for an Azure-heavy job posting, leading with your Spark
experience for a big-data-heavy one).
```

steps.heading: Common Resume Mistakes That Get Candidates Screened Out
steps.body:
```
- Typos/inconsistent formatting (signals lack of attention to detail —
  a genuinely important DE trait)
- Buzzword soup with no evidence of actual depth ("expert in AI, ML,
  Big Data, Cloud, Blockchain...") — reads as unfocused/inflated
- No quantified impact anywhere — every bullet reads as a duty description
- Resume longer than 1-2 pages for most career stages (recruiters
  genuinely don't read a 4-page resume in the seconds they typically spend)
- Listing every single tool you've ever touched once, rather than the
  tools you're GENUINELY proficient in — this backfires badly if a
  technical interviewer asks a follow-up question about something
  listed but barely known
```

steps.heading: Interview Traps
steps.body:
- "Walk me through your resume" — practice a CONCISE (60-90 second), well-structured narrative of your background, not a rambling recitation of every bullet point.
- Be ready to speak in DEPTH about literally anything listed on your resume — if you list a tool, expect a follow-up question about it, and never list something you can't discuss genuinely.

12-interview-prep/03-behavioral-intervie.title: Behavioral Interview Mastery — STAR Method & The Real Questions Behind the Questions
12-interview-prep/03-behavioral-intervie.tagline: A technically brilliant candidate who's a poor teammate, can't communicate clearly, or shows no self-awareness about past mistakes is a genu…
learnItems: Why Behavioral Interviews Matter More Than Candidates Often Assume
The STAR Method — The Standard Structure
The Real Question Behind Common Behavioral Prompts
Preparing Your Story Bank (do this BEFORE any interview, not during)
A Genuinely Good Failure Story — What Makes It Strong

steps.heading: Why Behavioral Interviews Matter More Than Candidates Often Assume
steps.body: A technically brilliant candidate who's a poor teammate, can't communicate clearly, or shows no self-awareness about past mistakes is a genuine, common hiring risk — many companies weight behavioral rounds AS HEAVILY as technical ones, precisely because technical skill can often be taught/improved, while fundamental communication/collaboration patterns are harder to change quickly.

steps.heading: The STAR Method — The Standard Structure
steps.body:
```
Situation: brief context — what was the setting/challenge? (10-15 seconds)
Task: what were YOU specifically responsible for? (10-15 seconds)
Action: what did YOU actually do, step by step? (the BULK of your
        answer, 60-90 seconds — this is what interviewers are most
        listening for)
Result: what happened, ideally quantified, AND what you learned
        (10-20 seconds)
```
**Common STAR mistake**: spending 80% of the answer on Situation/Task (context-setting) and rushing through Action — the ACTION section, showing what YOU specifically did and how you thought about it, is what interviewers are actually evaluating.

steps.heading: The Real Question Behind Common Behavioral Prompts
steps.body:
```
"Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate/manager"
  Real question being tested: can you handle conflict professionally,
  advocate for your view with evidence rather than ego, and still
  maintain a good working relationship afterward?

"Tell me about a time you failed"
  Real question being tested: genuine self-awareness and ability to
  learn from mistakes — NOT looking for a fake-humble "failure" that's
  secretly a brag ("I just work too hard sometimes"); wants a REAL
  mistake with genuine reflection on what you'd do differently.

"Tell me about a time you had to learn something quickly"
  Real question being tested: your actual LEARNING PROCESS — do you
  have a genuine, repeatable approach to picking up new skills/tools,
  relevant to the fast-evolving nature of data engineering tools
  (recap this repo's own "latest tech" emphasis throughout).

"Tell me about a time you had to make a decision with incomplete information"
  Real question being tested: directly connects to module 11's
  requirements-gathering and tradeoff-articulation skills — a strong
  answer demonstrates the SAME reasoning process taught throughout
  that module, applied to a real situation.

"Why do you want to work here / why are you leaving your current role"
  Real question being tested: genuine, thoughtful motivation vs a
  generic answer that could apply to any company — do genuine research
  on the SPECIFIC company beforehand.
```

steps.heading: Preparing Your Story Bank (do this BEFORE any interview, not during)
steps.body:
```
A genuinely effective practice: prepare 6-8 REAL stories from your
experience covering different themes (a conflict, a failure, a
technical challenge, a leadership moment, a time you influenced without
authority, a time you had to learn fast) — then MAP each specific
interview question you encounter to the closest-fitting story from
your bank, rather than trying to invent a new story on the spot.
```

steps.heading: A Genuinely Good Failure Story — What Makes It Strong
steps.body:
```
WEAK: "I once missed a deadline because the scope was unclear" (vague,
      no real ownership, blames circumstances)

STRONG: "I built a pipeline that seemed to work in testing, but I
        hadn't tested against a specific edge case in real production
        data — it silently corrupted about 2% of records for 3 days
        before we caught it via a downstream data quality alert. I
        took ownership of the fix, wrote a reconciliation query to
        identify and correct the affected records, and — more
        importantly — added the specific edge-case test to our test
        suite AND proposed a broader review of our testing practices
        with representative production-like data (recap
        `10-devops/08`'s DE-specific testing discussion), which the
        team adopted for future pipelines."
```
This works because it: shows a REAL mistake (not a disguised brag), demonstrates OWNERSHIP (fixed it personally), shows LEARNING (specific, concrete process change), and connects to genuine technical understanding (testing with representative data) — exactly the kind of substantive, technically-grounded story that distinguishes strong behavioral answers.

steps.heading: Handling "Do You Have Any Questions For Us?" (never skip this)
steps.body:
```
Genuinely asking thoughtful questions signals real engagement and
helps YOU evaluate the role/team too. Strong questions:
- "What does the data platform's current architecture look like, and
  what's the biggest pain point the team is trying to solve in the
  next year?" (shows genuine technical curiosity)
- "How does the team currently balance new feature work vs technical
  debt/platform improvements?" (shows mature, senior-level thinking)
- "What does success look like for this role in the first 6 months?"

AVOID asking questions you could easily find on the company's public
website (signals lack of preparation).
```

steps.heading: Interview Traps
steps.body:
- Never give a behavioral answer with NO specific details ("I always communicate well with my team") — interviewers want a SPECIFIC, real situation, not a general character claim.
- If you genuinely don't have a strong example for a specific question, it's better to briefly acknowledge and pivot to your CLOSEST relevant experience ("I haven't faced that exact scenario, but a related situation was...") than to force an unconvincing story.
- Practice your story bank OUT LOUD, not just mentally — verbalizing reveals where a story is actually unclear or too long in a way silent rehearsal doesn't.

12-interview-prep/04-technical-screening.title: Technical Screening Prep — What's Actually Being Tested
learnItems: What a Typical Technical Screen Covers
What the Interviewer Is ACTUALLY Evaluating (beyond correctness)
A Concrete Strategy for Live SQL Problems
A Concrete Strategy for Live Python/Coding Problems
What to Do When You Don't Know Something

steps.heading: What a Typical Technical Screen Covers
steps.body:
```
Usually 45-60 minutes, commonly structured as:
- 5-10 min: brief background discussion/resume walkthrough
- 20-30 min: live SQL and/or Python coding
- 10-15 min: possibly a lightweight system design or conceptual
  discussion question
- 5-10 min: your questions for them
```

steps.heading: What the Interviewer Is ACTUALLY Evaluating (beyond correctness)
steps.body:
```
- Can you translate a WORD PROBLEM into correct SQL/Python without
  extensive hand-holding? (recap the pattern-recognition skill
  emphasized throughout `02-sql/` — "this smells like a window
  function problem")
- Do you communicate your THINKING as you work, or go silent? (silence
  makes it impossible for an interviewer to give you partial credit or
  help redirect you if you're heading down a wrong path)
- How do you handle being STUCK? (asking a clarifying question,
  thinking out loud about approaches, vs freezing or guessing randomly)
- Do you consider EDGE CASES proactively? (nulls, duplicates, empty
  results — recap the production-mindset emphasis throughout this repo)
- Can you EXPLAIN your own solution afterward, including its
  complexity/performance characteristics?
```

steps.heading: A Concrete Strategy for Live SQL Problems
steps.body:
```
1. RESTATE the problem in your own words first ("So I need to find
   the second-highest salary per department, correct?") — confirms
   understanding AND buys yourself a moment to think

2. Think OUT LOUD about the APPROACH before writing code ("I'm
   thinking I'll use a window function here, DENSE_RANK specifically,
   because...") — recap `02-sql/05`'s pattern-recognition approach

3. Write the query INCREMENTALLY, narrating as you go, rather than
   going silent for 5 minutes and presenting a finished block

4. TEST your own query mentally against a small example BEFORE
   declaring it done ("let me trace through this with a small example...")

5. Proactively mention EDGE CASES even if not explicitly asked
   ("this would need to handle ties in salary — let me make sure
   DENSE_RANK handles that correctly...")
```

steps.heading: A Concrete Strategy for Live Python/Coding Problems
steps.body:
```
1. Clarify INPUT/OUTPUT format and constraints explicitly before coding
   ("Can this list contain duplicates? Can it be empty?")

2. Discuss your APPROACH and its rough complexity BEFORE writing code
   ("I could do this with a nested loop, O(n²), or use a dictionary
   for O(n) — let me go with the dictionary approach for efficiency")

3. Write clean, reasonably well-named code — even under time pressure,
   avoid single-letter variable names that obscure your own reasoning
   for the interviewer watching

4. Test with a SIMPLE example, then explicitly consider an EDGE CASE
   (empty input, single element, all-duplicate values)

5. If genuinely stuck, narrate your stuck-ness rather than going silent
   ("I'm not immediately seeing the cleanest approach here — let me
   think through a brute-force version first, then see if I can optimize")
```

steps.heading: What to Do When You Don't Know Something
steps.body:
```
NEVER bluff/pretend confidence about something you don't actually know
— technical interviewers can usually tell, and it erodes trust in
everything ELSE you say. Instead:
  "I haven't worked directly with [X], but based on [related concept
  I DO know], I'd guess it works similarly to... — is that roughly right?"
This demonstrates genuine intellectual honesty AND an ability to reason
from related knowledge — often scores BETTER than a candidate who
happens to know the exact answer but can't explain their reasoning.
```

steps.heading: Practicing Effectively (not just solving problems silently)
steps.body:
```
The single highest-leverage practice technique: solve problems OUT
LOUD, as if explaining to an interviewer, even when practicing alone —
silent problem-solving builds a DIFFERENT skill than verbalized,
interview-realistic problem-solving, and many otherwise-strong
candidates struggle specifically with the VERBALIZATION skill under
pressure, not the underlying technical knowledge itself.
```

steps.heading: Interview Traps
steps.body:
- Going completely silent while coding is one of the most common ways technical screens go poorly for genuinely competent candidates — practice narrating your thought process as an explicit, deliberate skill, not an afterthought.
- Don't immediately start typing/writing code the instant a question is given — take the 10-30 seconds to actually think through an approach and communicate it first; rushing to code often leads to a wrong first attempt that costs MORE time than the upfront thinking would have.
- If you make a mistake mid-solution, calmly acknowledge and fix it ("wait, I think I have an off-by-one error here, let me check...") rather than pretending it didn't happen — self-correction is a POSITIVE signal, not a negative one.

recapPoints: What a Typical Technical Screen Covers

12-interview-prep/05-live-coding-sql-pyt.title: Live Coding Strategy — SQL & Python, Deep Practice Approach
12-interview-prep/05-live-coding-sql-pyt.tagline: The single biggest jump in live SQL interview performance comes from recognizing WHICH pattern a problem needs, quickly:
learnItems: The Pattern-Recognition Skill (the real thing being tested, recap module 02)
A Structured SQL Practice Routine
Python Live Coding — What Actually Gets Asked for DE Roles (different from a typical SWE algorithm interview)
A Genuinely Useful Practice Habit: the "Explain It to a Rubber Duck" Technique
Handling Interviewer Hints (a skill in itself)

steps.heading: The Pattern-Recognition Skill (the real thing being tested, recap module 02)
steps.body:
The single biggest jump in live SQL interview performance comes from recognizing WHICH pattern a problem needs, quickly:
```
"Find the Nth highest/per-group X" -> window function (DENSE_RANK), recap `02-sql/05`
"Remove duplicates, keep latest" -> ROW_NUMBER + PARTITION, recap `02-sql/06`
"Find records in A but not B" -> LEFT JOIN + IS NULL, or NOT EXISTS, recap `02-sql/02` and `04`
"Consecutive streak/gaps" -> the row-number-minus-date trick, recap `02-sql/06`
"Compare to previous row" -> LAG/LEAD, recap `02-sql/05`
"Running total" -> SUM() OVER, recap `02-sql/05`
```
Practicing enough PROBLEMS that you recognize these patterns INSTANTLY (rather than re-deriving the approach from scratch each time) is the single highest-leverage SQL interview prep activity.

steps.heading: A Structured SQL Practice Routine
steps.body:
```
Week 1-2: Drill the FUNDAMENTALS until automatic — joins, aggregation,
          subqueries (recap `02-sql/01-04`) — speed and confidence here
          frees up mental bandwidth for harder problems later

Week 3-4: Drill WINDOW FUNCTIONS specifically — this is consistently
          the single most-tested SQL topic at product companies
          (recap `02-sql/05`) — practice until RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs
          ROW_NUMBER differences are completely automatic

Week 5-6: Drill the ADVANCED PATTERNS — dedup, gaps/islands,
          sessionization, cohort analysis (recap `02-sql/06`) —
          these show up constantly at product companies specifically
          (recap the case studies in `02-sql/case-studies/`)

Ongoing: mix in the REAL COMPANY CASE STUDIES from `02-sql/case-studies/`
         specifically — practicing recognizing "this is a funnel
         analysis problem" or "this is a cohort retention problem" from
         a business scenario description, not just a pre-labeled SQL exercise
```

steps.heading: Python Live Coding — What Actually Gets Asked for DE Roles (different from a typical SWE algorithm interview)
steps.body:
```
DE-specific Python interviews commonly focus on:
- Data manipulation problems (often solvable with EITHER plain Python
  OR pandas — being ready to discuss both approaches is valuable)
- Parsing/transforming semi-structured data (nested JSON/dicts — recap
  `03-python/01`'s dict/list manipulation fluency)
- Writing a function with proper error handling (recap `03-python/02`)
  — some interviewers SPECIFICALLY check whether you handle errors
  gracefully without being explicitly told to
- Less commonly (but sometimes): a classic algorithm problem (sorting,
  searching, basic data structures) — worth SOME practice, but usually
  less central to DE-specific interviews than pure SWE interviews
```

steps.heading: A Genuinely Useful Practice Habit: the "Explain It to a Rubber Duck" Technique
steps.body:
```
Before writing ANY code in practice, say OUT LOUD (or write in a
comment) your full plan: "First I'll do X, then Y, then handle the Z
edge case" — this single habit, practiced repeatedly, is what builds
the narration skill that live coding interviews specifically reward,
far more than just solving MORE problems silently ever will.
```

steps.heading: Handling Interviewer Hints (a skill in itself)
steps.body:
```
If an interviewer gives you a hint ("have you considered using a
window function here?"), respond with genuine engagement, not
defensiveness: "Ah, good point — let me think about how that would
apply here..." and actually incorporate it, rather than stubbornly
continuing your original approach. Interviewers give hints SPECIFICALLY
to see how you respond to new information mid-problem — handling this
gracefully is itself a positive signal (directly connects to module 11's
"genuinely reconsider when pushed back on" lesson).
```

steps.heading: Interview Traps
steps.body:
- Practicing ONLY in a silent, no-pressure environment builds a different skill than what's tested live — practice with a timer, and ideally practice explaining solutions to another person (or recording yourself) at least a few times before a real interview.
- Don't memorize exact solutions to specific practice problems — memorize the PATTERNS (window function scenarios, join scenarios) so you can adapt to a NEW problem phrased differently, which is what real interviews actually present.
- If asked "what's the time complexity of this?" for a SQL query, be ready to reason about it in terms of indexes/scans (recap `02-sql/07`), not just Big-O notation from a pure algorithms context.

12-interview-prep/06-take-home-assignmen.title: Take-Home Assignment Strategy — What Separates Good From Great
12-interview-prep/06-take-home-assignmen.tagline: Take-home assignments let candidates demonstrate REALISTIC work quality (proper testing, documentation, thoughtful design) that's hard to sh…
learnItems: Why Companies Use Take-Homes
The #1 Mistake: Treating It as "Just Get the Right Answer"
A Genuinely Strong Take-Home Structure
Handling Ambiguity in the Assignment (a real, deliberate test)
Time Management — Don't Over-Invest, But Don't Under-Invest Either

steps.heading: Why Companies Use Take-Homes
steps.body: Take-home assignments let candidates demonstrate REALISTIC work quality (proper testing, documentation, thoughtful design) that's hard to show under live-interview time pressure — but they also genuinely evaluate whether you can work INDEPENDENTLY and make reasonable judgment calls without someone available to immediately clarify every ambiguity.

steps.heading: The #1 Mistake: Treating It as "Just Get the Right Answer"
steps.body:
```
A take-home asking you to "build a pipeline to process this sample
data" is testing MUCH more than whether your final output is correct:
- Did you handle edge cases (nulls, malformed rows, duplicates)
  PROACTIVELY, or does your code crash on anything not perfectly clean?
- Is your code STRUCTURED sensibly (functions, not one giant script —
  recap `03-python/13`'s production best practices), or a stream-of-
  consciousness script?
- Did you include ANY tests? (Even a few basic unit tests signal real
  production maturity, recap `10-devops/08`'s DE-specific testing discussion)
- Is there a README explaining your APPROACH and REASONING (recap
  module 11's tradeoff-articulation skill, applied in writing this time)?
- Did you handle ERRORS gracefully (recap `03-python/02`), or does an
  API timeout crash the whole thing with an ugly traceback?
```

steps.heading: A Genuinely Strong Take-Home Structure
steps.body:
```
project/
├── README.md          # approach, assumptions made, how to run it,
│                         and IMPORTANTLY, what you'd do differently
│                         with more time (shows self-awareness of
│                         tradeoffs, recap module 11's file 8)
├── src/
│   ├── extract.py
│   ├── transform.py
│   └── load.py
├── tests/
│   └── test_transform.py   # even 3-4 meaningful tests genuinely help
├── requirements.txt
└── sample_output/      # (if applicable) a small sample of your
                          actual output, so reviewers don't need to
                          run your code just to see what it produces
```

steps.heading: Handling Ambiguity in the Assignment (a real, deliberate test)
steps.body:
```
Take-home instructions are OFTEN deliberately somewhat ambiguous
(mirroring real work, where requirements are rarely perfectly specified)
— the RIGHT response is:
1. If a clarifying question is genuinely blocking, ask it (most
   companies welcome this, and it demonstrates good judgment about
   when to ask vs when to proceed)
2. For everything else, make a REASONABLE assumption, and EXPLICITLY
   DOCUMENT it in your README ("I assumed 'active user' means logged
   in within 30 days, since this wasn't specified") — this demonstrates
   EXACTLY the requirements-gathering instinct from module 11, applied
   independently without someone there to ask directly.
```

steps.heading: Time Management — Don't Over-Invest, But Don't Under-Invest Either
steps.body:
```
Most take-homes state an expected time budget (e.g., "should take
2-4 hours") — WILDLY exceeding this (spending 15 hours perfecting
something meant to take 3) can actually be viewed NEGATIVELY (poor
time-management judgment, or over-engineering relative to the actual
ask) — aim to deliver something GENUINELY solid within roughly the
stated budget, with your README explicitly noting what you'd add
with more time if relevant, rather than silently over-investing.
```

steps.heading: What to Do If You Genuinely Can't Finish Everything
steps.body:
```
A PARTIAL, well-documented, working solution with a clear README
explaining what's done, what's not, and WHY you prioritized what you
did, is almost always viewed better than a rushed, broken attempt at
the FULL scope — explicit, honest communication about scope tradeoffs
under time constraints is itself a positive signal (recap module 11's
emphasis on transparent reasoning).
```

steps.heading: Interview Traps
steps.body:
- Submitting code with ZERO tests, zero README, and zero error handling — even if the core logic is technically correct, this reads as "doesn't operate with production maturity," a genuine red flag for a DE role specifically.
- Wildly over-engineering a simple ask (e.g., setting up a full Kubernetes deployment for a take-home explicitly asking for "a simple script") — signals poor judgment about matching solution complexity to the actual ask (recap module 11 file 8's simplicity-argument instinct).
- Not reading the instructions carefully enough to catch an explicitly stated constraint (e.g., "must run without any paid API keys") — a surprisingly common, easily avoidable way to lose points regardless of code quality.

12-interview-prep/07-system-design-inter.title: System Design Interview Strategy — Applying Module 11, Live
12-interview-prep/07-system-design-inter.tagline: Module 11 taught you the REASONING (requirements, tradeoffs, capacity estimation, the 6-step framework). This file is specifically about the…
learnItems: This File's Purpose
Time Management in a 45-Minute System Design Round
Whiteboard/Diagram Communication (mechanics matter, not just content)
Handling "What If This Requirement Changed?" Follow-Ups
Common System Design Interview Formats (know which one you're in)

steps.heading: This File's Purpose
steps.body: Module 11 taught you the REASONING (requirements, tradeoffs, capacity estimation, the 6-step framework). This file is specifically about the INTERVIEW PERFORMANCE layer on top of that reasoning — time management, whiteboard/communication mechanics, and handling the live, interactive nature of this specific round.

steps.heading: Time Management in a 45-Minute System Design Round
steps.body:
```
Roughly:
5 min:  Requirements clarification (module 11 file 2) — don't rush this,
        but don't spend 20 minutes here either
5 min:  High-level data flow sketch (module 11 file 10, step 2)
5 min:  Capacity estimation (module 11 file 7) — narrate the math
20 min: Deep dive on specific components, WITH explicit tradeoff
        justification (module 11 files 3, 4, 8) — this is where MOST
        of your talking should happen
5 min:  Failure modes/scale discussion (module 11 file 6)
5 min:  Summary + inviting questions (module 11 file 10, step 6)

If the interviewer steers you toward spending MORE time on a specific
area (they often will, deliberately, to see how deep your knowledge
goes there), FOLLOW their lead — this isn't you failing to stick to a
plan, it's the interviewer actively probing where THEY want more depth.
```

steps.heading: Whiteboard/Diagram Communication (mechanics matter, not just content)
steps.body:
```
- Use CONSISTENT, simple shapes (boxes for services/components, arrows
  for data flow) — don't worry about making it visually beautiful,
  worry about making it CLEAR
- Label arrows with WHAT'S flowing ("order events," not just an
  unlabeled arrow) — this small habit dramatically improves clarity
- Leave VISUAL SPACE to add detail as the conversation goes deeper —
  don't cram your initial sketch so tightly that there's no room to
  annotate/extend it as the interviewer asks follow-ups
- If working in a shared doc/virtual whiteboard, keep your sketch
  visible/shared throughout — don't switch away from it while
  continuing to talk about it
```

steps.heading: Handling "What If This Requirement Changed?" Follow-Ups
steps.body:
```
This is one of the MOST COMMON and MOST IMPORTANT moments in a system
design interview — recap module 11 file 10's "handling pushback" guidance.

The interviewer changing a requirement mid-discussion ("what if this
needed to be real-time instead of daily batch?") is DELIBERATELY testing
whether you can genuinely RE-REASON, not just defend your original
design. Practice, explicitly:
"That changes [specific component] significantly, because [reasoning].
I'd now consider [specific alternative], accepting [new tradeoff]
instead of [old tradeoff]."
```

steps.heading: Common System Design Interview Formats (know which one you're in)
steps.body:
```
Open-ended prompt ("design a data platform for X"): most common,
  most similar to module 11's case studies — apply the full 6-step
  framework.

A more NARROW, specific prompt ("how would you design the incremental
  loading logic for this specific table"): requires LESS requirements-
  gathering ceremony and MORE immediate technical depth — read the
  scope of the question correctly and calibrate your depth-vs-breadth
  balance accordingly.

A "critique this existing design" prompt (less common, but does
  happen): requires you to identify SPECIFIC weaknesses/risks in a
  GIVEN design (recap module 11 file 4's "where will this break first"
  exercise) rather than designing from scratch.
```

steps.heading: What a Strong Closing Sounds Like
steps.body:
```
"So to summarize, given [key requirements], I've proposed [core
architecture], with [key technology choices] justified by [reasoning],
accepting [explicit tradeoff]. If I had more time, I'd want to dig
deeper into [specific area] — what would be most useful for you to
explore further?"

This demonstrates: synthesis ability, genuine tradeoff awareness, AND
appropriate humility about the depth achievable in 45 minutes — all
strong signals.
```

steps.heading: Interview Traps
steps.body:
- Don't treat a system design interview as a monologue — genuinely PAUSE periodically and invite the interviewer's input/questions; the BEST system design interviews feel like a collaborative discussion, not a one-person presentation.
- If the interviewer seems to want you to move faster through a section you're spending too long on, take that cue and move on — reading the room/interviewer's signals is itself part of what's being evaluated.
- Never present your FIRST idea as if it's obviously correct with no alternatives considered — even briefly mentioning "I considered X, but chose Y because..." demonstrates the tradeoff-awareness that module 11 emphasizes throughout.

12-interview-prep/08-negotiation-and-off.title: Negotiation & Offer Evaluation
12-interview-prep/08-negotiation-and-off.tagline: Total compensation components to actually consider:
learnItems: Evaluating an Offer — Beyond Just the Base Salary Number
How to Actually Negotiate (most candidates under-negotiate)
Comparing Multiple Offers (a genuinely common, good problem to have)
Red Flags to Watch For During the Process Itself (this is data too)
Interview Traps

steps.heading: Evaluating an Offer — Beyond Just the Base Salary Number
steps.body:
```
Total compensation components to actually consider:
- Base salary
- Bonus (target %, and REALISTIC historical payout — ask directly)
- Equity/stock (RSUs at a public company have a fairly clear value;
  options/equity at a private company/startup are genuinely
  speculative — understand vesting schedules and realistic outcomes)
- Benefits (health insurance quality, retirement matching, genuinely
  varies a lot and has real financial value)
- Signing bonus (often used to bridge a gap, sometimes with a
  clawback if you leave within a certain period — read the fine print)

Non-compensation factors genuinely worth weighing:
- Learning/growth trajectory (will this role build genuinely
  valuable, current skills — recap this repo's emphasis on staying
  current with evolving tools)
- Team/manager quality (arguably the single biggest factor in
  day-to-day job satisfaction, hard to assess but worth genuinely
  trying to via questions asked during the process)
- Company financial health/stability (especially relevant for
  smaller companies/startups)
- Work-life balance/on-call expectations (recap `08-orchestration/08`'s
  on-call reality discussion — worth asking directly about this for
  a DE role specifically)
```

steps.heading: How to Actually Negotiate (most candidates under-negotiate)
steps.body:
```
The single most important fact: MOST companies EXPECT some negotiation
and build a small amount of room into their initial offer — simply
ASKING (professionally) is far more likely to improve your offer than
NOT asking, and rarely backfires if done reasonably and respectfully.

A simple, effective negotiation approach:
"Thank you so much for the offer, I'm genuinely excited about this
role. Based on [my experience/market research/a competing offer, if
genuinely true], I was hoping we could explore [a specific number or
range] — is there flexibility here?"

Key principles:
- Be SPECIFIC (a number or range), not vague ("can you do better?")
- Have GENUINE justification ready (market research, a competing
  offer, specific relevant experience) — recruiters respond better to
  reasoned asks than pure assertion
- Negotiate the WHOLE package, not just base salary, if base has
  limited flexibility (sometimes signing bonus/equity/start date has
  more room to move)
- NEVER lie about a competing offer that doesn't exist — this is a
  genuinely risky, sometimes discoverable, and ethically poor practice
```

steps.heading: Comparing Multiple Offers (a genuinely common, good problem to have)
steps.body:
```
Beyond raw compensation, weigh:
- Which role builds skills most aligned with where you want your
  career to go in 2-3 years (recap module 11's senior/architect
  career-progression discussion)?
- Which team/manager did you get the STRONGEST genuine positive signal
  from during the process?
- Which company's technical stack/maturity genuinely excites you to
  work in daily (recap this repo's coverage of legacy vs modern stacks
  — some candidates genuinely prefer greenfield modern-stack work,
  others prefer the stability/scale of enterprise legacy environments)?
```

steps.heading: Red Flags to Watch For During the Process Itself (this is data too)
steps.body:
```
- A disorganized, unresponsive, or repeatedly-rescheduled interview
  process can be a genuine signal about internal team dysfunction
- Vague or evasive answers when YOU ask about on-call expectations,
  team turnover, or why the role is open
- Pressure to accept an offer with an unreasonably short deadline,
  without a genuine reason given
```

steps.heading: Interview Traps
steps.body:
- "What are your salary expectations?" (often asked EARLY, by the
  recruiter) — research market rates beforehand (levels.fyi, Glassdoor,
  and genuinely talking to people in similar roles) so you give a
  grounded, confident range rather than an uninformed guess or an
  overly-hesitant non-answer.
- Never accept an offer on the spot in the excitement of the moment if
  you have ANY genuine hesitation — it's completely normal and expected
  to ask for a few days to consider, even after a strong, exciting offer.

recapPoints: Evaluating an Offer — Beyond Just the Base Salary Number

12-interview-prep/09-90-day-study-plan.title: The 90-Day Study Plan — Using This Entire Repo Systematically
12-interview-prep/09-90-day-study-plan.tagline: Someone with SOME existing background (not necessarily a total beginner) who has roughly 3 months before actively interviewing, and wants a …
learnItems: Who This Plan Is For

Weeks 4-6: The Full Tool Stack (Modules 03-06)
Weeks 7-9: Scale, Cloud, and Operations (Modules 06-10)

steps.heading: Who This Plan Is For
steps.body: Someone with SOME existing background (not necessarily a total beginner) who has roughly 3 months before actively interviewing, and wants a structured way to move through this entire repo rather than randomly jumping between modules.

steps.heading: Weeks 1-3: Foundations Solid (Modules 01, 02, 03)
steps.body:
```
Week 1: 01-fundamentals (ALL of it) — this is the conceptual vocabulary
        everything else builds on; do not skip this even if some of it
        feels basic, since interview questions constantly reference
        these foundational concepts (SCD, OLTP/OLAP, CAP theorem, etc.)

Week 2: 02-sql files 1-6 (basics through advanced patterns) — practice
        EVERY query in the playground; this is genuinely the most
        heavily-tested single skill area

Week 3: 02-sql files 7-9 + case studies + interview questions
        (optimization, transactions, production) — THEN 03-python
        files 1-5 (fundamentals through database connectivity)
```

steps.heading: Weeks 4-6: The Full Tool Stack (Modules 03-06)
steps.body:
```
Week 4: 03-python files 6-13 (APIs, cloud SDKs, SharePoint/Graph API,
        PySpark intro, data quality, production practices) — this is
        where "book knowledge" starts becoming "can actually build things"

Week 5: 04-etl-elt (all of it) — understanding WHY tools evolved this
        way (SSIS/Informatica -> ADF/Glue/dbt) builds genuine judgment,
        not just tool syntax memorization

Week 6: 05-databases (all of it) — this is a DENSE module; don't rush
        it, especially the history/evolution files and the "what
        companies actually use" file, which come up constantly in
        interviews
```

steps.heading: Weeks 7-9: Scale, Cloud, and Operations (Modules 06-10)
steps.body:
```
Week 7: 06-big-data (all of it) — Spark internals and performance
        tuning specifically deserve real attention here, a very
        commonly-probed depth area in interviews

Week 8: 07-cloud-platforms (all of it) — pick whichever cloud is most
        relevant to your target jobs and go DEEPEST there, while still
        reading the others for breadth/comparison fluency

Week 9: 08-orchestration + 09-visualization + 10-devops — these three
        together build your "how does this actually run in production"
        fluency; don't skip DevOps even if it feels adjacent to "real"
        DE work — it's increasingly expected knowledge
```

steps.heading: Weeks 10-12: System Design & Interview Execution (Modules 11-12)
steps.body:
```
Week 10: 11-system-design files 1-10 — read slowly, this is the
         highest-leverage material for senior-level interviews
         specifically; do the "try it yourself" exercises genuinely,
         don't just read passively

Week 11: Work through ALL 7 case studies in 11-system-design/case-studies/
         YOURSELF FIRST (blank page, no peeking) before comparing your
         reasoning to the provided walkthroughs — this is where real
         judgment gets built, not from reading alone

Week 12: 12-interview-prep (this module) — resume/portfolio polish,
         behavioral story bank preparation, and final review of the
         master-question-bank.md across all modules
```

steps.heading: A Parallel Track to Run THROUGHOUT All 12 Weeks
steps.body:
```
- Build/maintain a real portfolio project (recap file 2) incrementally
  — don't leave this until week 12
- Do 15-20 minutes of SQL practice most days (small, consistent
  practice beats occasional long cram sessions for pattern-recognition
  automaticity, recap file 5)
- Keep a running personal "story bank" document (file 3) — add a new
  behavioral story draft whenever you recall a genuinely relevant
  past experience, rather than trying to invent 8 stories from
  scratch in week 12
```

steps.heading: Adjusting This Plan for Your Situation
steps.body:
```
Less time available (e.g., 4 weeks, an urgent job search):
  Compress to: 02-sql (critical) -> 03-python essentials ->
  05-databases key concepts -> 11-system-design (files 1, 2, 8, 10 +
  at least 3 case studies) -> 12-interview-prep — accept you won't
  go as deep everywhere, prioritize breadth of the MOST commonly-tested areas

More experienced, targeting senior/staff roles specifically:
  Spend disproportionately MORE time in 11-system-design and the
  "what companies actually use" files across every module (05, 06, 07,
  08, 09, 10) — these are exactly what differentiates senior-level
  interview performance, per module 11 file 9's discussion
```

steps.heading: Interview Traps
steps.body:
- Don't treat this plan as rigid — if a specific job posting emphasizes a particular skill (e.g., heavy Kafka/streaming focus), REORDER to prioritize that area regardless of the "default" week sequence above.
- The parallel portfolio-building track is not optional filler — it's what makes your resume (file 2) and your interview stories (file 3) genuinely CONCRETE rather than abstract, and interviewers can tell the difference.

12-interview-prep/10-common-mistakes-and.title: Common Mistakes & Red Flags — From Both Sides of the Table
12-interview-prep/10-common-mistakes-and.tagline: first (recap file 4/5's emphasis on restating/clarifying before coding)
learnItems: Candidate Mistakes That Actually Fail Interviews (compiled patterns)
Red Flags to Watch For as a CANDIDATE Evaluating the Company (this cuts both ways)
The Single Biggest Meta-Mistake (across every round type)
Interview Traps

steps.heading: Candidate Mistakes That Actually Fail Interviews (compiled patterns)
steps.body:
### Technical Rounds
```
- Jumping straight to code/a solution without clarifying the problem
  first (recap file 4/5's emphasis on restating/clarifying before coding)
- Going completely silent while working through a problem, leaving the
  interviewer unable to follow your reasoning or offer a helpful nudge
- Presenting a solution as finished without testing it against even
  a simple example first
- Bluffing confidently about something you don't actually know, rather
  than honestly reasoning from related knowledge (recap file 4's
  guidance on this)
- Ignoring edge cases entirely unless EXPLICITLY prompted for them
```

### System Design Rounds
```
- Skipping requirements clarification and diving straight into "we'll
  use Kafka + Spark + Snowflake" (recap module 11 file 1's junior-vs-
  senior comparison — this is THE most common way candidates read as
  junior regardless of actual seniority)
- Presenting a design with NO explicit tradeoffs mentioned, as if the
  chosen approach has no cost at all (recap module 11 file 8)
- Defending an initial design rigidly when the interviewer pushes back
  with new information, rather than genuinely re-reasoning (recap
  module 11 file 10's pushback-handling guidance)
- Reflexively choosing the most sophisticated/trendy technology without
  justifying it against the STATED requirements
```

### Behavioral Rounds
```
- Vague, non-specific answers with no concrete situation described
  (recap file 3)
- A "failure" story that's secretly a humblebrag with no genuine
  learning shown
- Badmouthing a previous employer/manager — even if genuinely justified,
  this reads poorly and raises concern about how you'd speak about
  THIS company later
- No prepared questions when asked "do you have any questions for us"
  — signals a lack of genuine engagement/curiosity
```

### Process/Communication
```
- Being unresponsive/slow to schedule or reply during the process
  itself (a real, if informal, signal recruiters/hiring managers
  genuinely factor in)
- Not following up with a brief, genuine thank-you note after
  interviews — small, but a real, low-cost positive signal
- Being dishonest about experience/skills that get exposed by a
  follow-up technical question — far more damaging than honestly
  saying "I haven't worked with that specifically"
```

steps.heading: Red Flags to Watch For as a CANDIDATE Evaluating the Company (this cuts both ways)
steps.body:
```
- Interviewers who can't clearly articulate what the team is currently
  working on or why the role is open (signals internal disorganization)
- Evasiveness about on-call expectations, team turnover, or why the
  previous person in this role left
- A consistently disorganized, repeatedly-rescheduled interview process
- Pressure tactics (unreasonably short offer deadlines with no
  legitimate reason given)
- Job posting/interview descriptions of the role that shift
  significantly and inconsistently across different interviewers you
  speak with (signals the role/team may not have a clear, agreed
  mandate internally)
```

steps.heading: The Single Biggest Meta-Mistake (across every round type)
steps.body:
```
Treating an interview as a TEST TO PASS rather than a GENUINE TWO-WAY
CONVERSATION to determine mutual fit. Candidates who genuinely engage
with curiosity (asking real questions, showing authentic interest in
HOW a company solves problems, being honestly reflective in behavioral
answers) consistently outperform candidates treating it as a
memorized-answer performance — this shows up subtly across EVERY
round type covered in this module, and interviewers, even without
being able to fully articulate why, consistently rate genuine
engagement higher than rehearsed perfection.
```

steps.heading: Interview Traps
steps.body: - If you notice yourself making one of these candidate mistakes DURING an actual interview (e.g., realizing you've gone silent for too long, or that you're defending a position too rigidly), it's genuinely fine to self-correct in the moment ("let me back up and think through this differently") — self-awareness demonstrated LIVE is itself a strong, positive signal, not an admission of failure.

- ETL vs ELT
- Batch vs Streaming
- SQL vs NoSQL (for a specific access pattern)
- Star schema vs Data Vault
- Lambda vs Kappa architecture
- Reserved vs Serverless cloud pricing
- Centralized vs Data Mesh data platform ownership
- Build vs Buy for a data tool

steps.heading: Final Reminder
steps.body:
```
This entire repo — 12 modules, hundreds of files — exists to build ONE
thing: genuine, flexible, articulable JUDGMENT about data engineering
problems. The specific facts/syntax matter less than the ability to
REASON through something you haven't seen exactly before, using the
patterns and frameworks built throughout this repo. Trust the process,
practice articulating your reasoning out loud, and walk into your
interview ready to have a genuine conversation, not recite memorized answers.

Good luck. 🚀
```

12-interview-prep/case-mock-system-desig.title: Case Study: A Full Mock System Design Interview, Annotated
12-interview-prep/case-mock-system-desig.tagline: *A realistic transcript-style walkthrough showing good technique applied live, with annotations explaining WHY each moment works, tying back…
learnItems: Overview
Why This Transcript Demonstrates Strong Performance

steps.heading: Overview
steps.body:
*A realistic transcript-style walkthrough showing good technique applied live, with annotations explaining WHY each moment works, tying back to modules 11 and 12.*

**Prompt given by interviewer**: "Design a data pipeline for a company that wants to analyze customer support ticket data to identify trending issues."

---

**Candidate**: "Great, before I dive in, I'd like to ask a few clarifying questions. First, what does 'identify trending issues' actually mean in practice — is this a dashboard the support team checks periodically, or does it need to trigger real-time alerts for a sudden spike in a specific issue type?"


**Interviewer**: "Good question — let's say it's mainly a dashboard the support team checks each morning, but they've also mentioned wanting to be alerted if something spikes dramatically during the day."

**Candidate**: "Got it — so we have two distinct needs: a daily/batch dashboard for the regular morning review, and a faster-turnaround anomaly detection for dramatic spikes during the day. That's helpful. A couple more quick questions: roughly what volume of tickets are we talking about, and where does ticket data currently live — a specific support tool like Zendesk, or a custom system?"

> *Annotation: Notice the candidate explicitly SUMMARIZES what they just learned ("so we have two distinct needs") before asking the next question — this demonstrates active listening and synthesis, not just question-firing.*

**Interviewer**: "About 50,000 tickets a month, and yes, it's Zendesk."

**Candidate**: "Okay, let me do some quick rough math. 50,000 tickets a month is roughly 1,700 a day, so under 1 event per second on average — genuinely modest volume. That tells me we don't need heavyweight streaming infrastructure purely for THROUGHPUT reasons — but we DO have that stated need for same-day spike detection, so let me think about how to satisfy that without over-engineering the whole pipeline."

> *Annotation: Explicit capacity estimation, narrated out loud (module 11 file 7 / file 10 Step 3), AND the candidate is already reasoning toward NOT defaulting to full streaming just because "trending/spike" sounds real-time-ish — a genuinely senior instinct (module 11 file 8's simplicity argument).*

**Candidate**: "Here's what I'm thinking at a high level: extract ticket data from Zendesk's API on a schedule — say, every 15 minutes, not truly real-time streaming — land it in a data lake, run it through a classification/categorization step to tag tickets by issue type, and then have two downstream paths: a nightly aggregation feeding the morning dashboard, and a lightweight check after each 15-minute extraction that compares today's issue-type volumes against a rolling baseline, alerting if something's a significant outlier."

> *Annotation: A clean high-level data flow (Step 2), and notice the SPECIFIC tradeoff being made explicit: 15-minute polling instead of true streaming, directly justified by the modest volume and the "same-day, not sub-second" actual latency requirement from Step 1.*

**Interviewer**: "That sounds reasonable. What if I told you the company is expecting to 10x their support volume next year through a big product launch?"

**Candidate**: "That's an important constraint to factor in now rather than after the fact. At 10x, we're looking at roughly 17,000 tickets a day, still under 1 event per second on average even then — so actually, I don't think this specific volume growth changes my core architecture much, since Zendesk's API and a simple lake-based pipeline can comfortably handle that. Where I WOULD want to double check is whether the 15-minute polling frequency against Zendesk's API has any rate-limit concerns at that volume, and whether the classification step — if it's using any kind of ML model — has enough throughput headroom. But I wouldn't jump to full streaming infrastructure just because of a 10x volume number alone, since even at that scale we're still in a genuinely modest range."

> *Annotation: This is THE critical moment (module 11 file 10's pushback-handling). The candidate does NOT panic and switch to "well then we definitely need Kafka" reflexively — they RE-DO the math live, show it still supports the simpler choice, and specifically identify the REAL risk areas (API rate limits, model throughput) worth double-checking instead. This demonstrates genuine reasoning, not a rehearsed answer, and resists the common pull toward reflexive over-engineering.*

**Interviewer**: "Good reasoning. How would you handle a ticket that gets updated multiple times as it moves through different statuses?"

**Candidate**: "That's an idempotency/deduplication concern — I'd want each extraction pull to capture the ticket's CURRENT state, keyed by ticket ID, and use an upsert pattern when landing it — so if the same ticket is pulled in three consecutive 15-minute windows because it's still open and being updated, we don't create three separate conflicting records, we just have the latest state reflected. I'd also keep the RAW extracted snapshots in a separate append-only landing zone specifically so we retain full history if we ever need to reconstruct a ticket's status timeline for analysis, even though the main aggregation table just reflects current state."

> *Annotation: Directly connects to idempotency (recap `01-fundamentals/02` and module 11 file 6) and demonstrates the Bronze/Silver layering instinct (recap module 11 file 3's Medallion discussion) — proactively, without the interviewer needing to explicitly ask "how do you handle historical reconstruction."*

**Candidate (wrapping up)**: "So to summarize — given the modest actual ticket volume and the stated need for same-day (not sub-second) spike detection, I'm proposing a 15-minute batch extraction from Zendesk into a lake, with an idempotent upsert pattern for ticket updates, feeding both a nightly full aggregation for the morning dashboard and a lightweight rolling-baseline comparison for intraday spike alerts. The main tradeoff is NOT building true real-time streaming infrastructure, which I think is justified by the actual requirements and volume here — though if the business's alerting needs tighten toward true real-time in the future, or if we hit real API rate-limit constraints at higher scale, I'd revisit that decision. steps.heading: What Data Governance Actually Means (Beyond the Buzzword)
steps.body: Data Governance is the overall system of DECISION RIGHTS, POLICIES, and ACCOUNTABILITY that determines how an organization's data is collected, classified, secured, accessed, and used — answering "who is allowed to do what with which data, and who is accountable if it goes wrong." It's not a single tool; it's a discipline that TOOLS (Purview, Glue Catalog, IAM) help enforce.

steps.heading: Why This Became Business-Critical (Not Just "Nice to Have")
steps.body:
```
- Regulatory fines are genuinely large and enforced: GDPR fines can
  reach 4% of GLOBAL annual revenue for serious violations — a real,
  board-level financial risk, not an abstract compliance checkbox
- High-profile data breaches/misuse scandals have made customers and
  regulators genuinely more scrutinous of how companies handle data
- As companies adopt AI/ML at scale, UNGOVERNED data becomes a direct
  liability — a model trained on improperly-sourced or biased data
  creates real legal and reputational exposure
```

steps.heading: The Core Regulations Every Data Engineer Should Understand (conceptually, not as a lawyer)
steps.body:
### GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation — EU, 2018)
```
Key principles a Data Engineer must design around:
- Right to Access: a user can request ALL data a company holds about them
- Right to Erasure ("right to be forgotten"): a user can request their
  data be DELETED — this has REAL pipeline design implications (can
  you actually find and delete a specific person's data across every
  system, including backups and derived/aggregated tables?)
- Data Minimization: collect only what's genuinely needed, not "just in case"
- Purpose Limitation: data collected for one purpose can't be silently
  repurposed for another without new consent
- Data Residency: personal data of EU citizens often has geographic
  storage/processing constraints (recap `07-cloud-platforms/09`'s
  region-selection discussion)
```

### CCPA/CPRA (California Consumer Privacy Act — US)
```
Similar spirit to GDPR (right to know, right to delete, right to
opt-out of data sale) but with different specific mechanics and
narrower geographic scope (California residents) — many US companies
design ONE compliant system that satisfies BOTH GDPR and CCPA
simultaneously rather than building separate systems per regulation.
```

### HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act — US healthcare)
```
Governs Protected Health Information (PHI) specifically — stricter
access logging, encryption, and audit trail requirements than general
PII; directly relevant to the healthcare case study pattern seen in
`06-big-data/06` (Delta Lake time travel for compliance) and this
module's own case study.
```

### PCI-DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard)
```
Governs how payment card data is stored/transmitted/processed — directly
relevant to the "isolated payments database" design decision in the
ride-hailing case study (`05-databases/case-studies/`) — PCI-DSS is
part of WHY that isolation is a genuinely standard real-world practice,
not just a performance optimization.
```

steps.heading: Data Classification — The Practical Starting Point
steps.body:
```
Before you can govern data, you must CLASSIFY it. A standard framework:

PUBLIC: no restriction (a public blog post, published pricing)
INTERNAL: for employees only, low sensitivity (an internal wiki page)
CONFIDENTIAL: business-sensitive, restricted (financial forecasts,
               unreleased product plans)
RESTRICTED/PII/PHI/PCI: highest sensitivity, legally regulated
   (customer SSNs, health records, credit card numbers, precise
   location history)

Every table/column in a data platform should ideally be TAGGED with
its classification level (recap the data catalog discussion in file 2)
— this tagging is what makes automated policy enforcement (masking,
access control, retention rules) possible at scale, rather than
manually tracking sensitivity in someone's head.
```

steps.heading: PII Specifically — What Counts (broader than people assume)
steps.body:
```
Direct identifiers: name, SSN/national ID, email, phone number

Indirect/quasi-identifiers (can identify someone when COMBINED):
  ZIP code + birth date + gender has been shown to uniquely identify
  the majority of the US population EVEN WITHOUT a name — a genuinely
  important, often-missed nuance: PII isn't just "obviously personal"
  fields, it's anything that COULD identify an individual, especially
  in combination with other fields.

This is why anonymization/pseudonymization requires real care (see
below) — simply removing the "obvious" name/email column is often
NOT sufficient to make data genuinely non-identifying.
```

steps.heading: Anonymization, Pseudonymization, and Masking — Real Techniques
steps.body:
```
Masking: replacing sensitive values with a fixed pattern for display
  purposes (e.g., showing "****-****-****-1234" for a credit card) —
  reversible IF the underlying real value is stored separately and
  securely.

Pseudonymization: replacing an identifier with a consistent token
  (e.g., customer_id 12345 always maps to token "a8f3e2") — the
  MAPPING is stored securely and separately, so the data is only
  re-identifiable by someone with access to that mapping — commonly
  used so analysts can still JOIN/aggregate data by customer without
  ever seeing real identifying information.

Anonymization (true): irreversibly removing the ability to
  re-identify an individual — genuinely much harder to achieve
  correctly than most people assume (recap the ZIP+birthdate+gender
  example above) — techniques like k-anonymity (ensuring any record
  is indistinguishable from at least k-1 others) and differential
  privacy (adding calibrated statistical noise) are the rigorous,
  mathematically-grounded approaches real privacy engineering uses.
```
```sql
-- A practical pseudonymization pattern in a dbt staging model
SELECT
    {{ dbt_utils.generate_surrogate_key(['customer_id']) }} AS customer_token,
    -- real customer_id is NEVER exposed past this staging layer
    order_amount,
    order_date
FROM {{ source('raw', 'orders') }}
```

steps.heading: Data Stewardship & Ownership — The Organizational Layer
steps.body:
```
Data Owner: typically a business-side role (e.g., "VP of Sales owns
  customer data") — accountable for defining WHO should have access
  and WHY, and for the data's overall quality/appropriate use

Data Steward: typically a more hands-on, often technical role — actually
  maintains documentation, classification tags, and quality rules for
  specific datasets day-to-day, reporting to/coordinating with the Data Owner

Data Custodian: the team (often Data Engineering itself) responsible
  for the TECHNICAL implementation of access controls, encryption, and
  retention — executing the policies Owners/Stewards define, not
  necessarily deciding them unilaterally
```
This three-role separation (Owner decides policy, Steward maintains day-to-day documentation/quality, Custodian implements technically) is a genuinely important organizational pattern — Data Engineers are usually Custodians, sometimes Stewards, rarely the sole Owner of a business dataset's governance policy.

steps.heading: Data Retention Policies — How Long to Keep What
steps.body:
```
A genuinely important, often-neglected practice: define EXPLICIT
retention rules per data classification/type, not "keep everything forever":
  - Transactional/financial data: often 7 years (tax/audit requirements)
  - Marketing engagement data: often much shorter (e.g., 1-2 years),
    balanced against genuine analytical value
  - Raw clickstream/log data: often has its OWN shorter retention than
    aggregated/summarized derivatives (keep detailed raw data for a
    bounded window, keep aggregates indefinitely)

Implemented technically via S3/ADLS lifecycle policies (recap
`07-cloud-platforms/03`) combined with warehouse table-level retention
configuration — governance POLICY driving technical IMPLEMENTATION,
exactly the Owner->Steward->Custodian chain above in action.
```

steps.heading: Interview Traps
steps.body:
- "What's the difference between anonymization and pseudonymization?" — pseudonymization is reversible with access to a secure mapping (enables joins/aggregation while hiding identity from most users); true anonymization aims to be irreversible, and is genuinely harder to achieve correctly than simply removing "obvious" identifying columns.
- "How would you design a pipeline to support GDPR's 'right to be forgotten'?" — needs a way to trace and delete a specific individual's data across ALL systems (raw, staged, aggregated, even backups) — a genuinely hard system design problem worth discussing thoughtfully rather than a one-line answer.
- "What's the difference between a Data Owner and a Data Steward?" — Owner is typically business-side, accountable for policy decisions; Steward is a more hands-on role maintaining day-to-day documentation/quality/classification.
